questions.prompt: What does "system of record" mean, as this course uses the term?
options: The single system treated as authoritative for a specific data element, decided per field rather than per system as a whole
The system with the most total records stored in it
The system that was implemented first, historically
The system a company's IT department prefers for licensing reasons
A system that only stores read-only, archived data
The system with the fastest response time
questions.explain: System of record is decided field by field -- it's about which system is authoritative for a specific piece of data, not a label applied to a whole system or chosen for unrelated reasons like speed or history.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B describes storage volume, which has nothing to do with authority over a specific data element. A system can hold the most records and still not be the authoritative source for any single field that matters to the integration.

questions.prompt: At Meridian Fixtures (Lesson 1), why does the design use a real-time callout for inventory and credit hold but a scheduled batch sync for catalog and price?
options: Because the ERP can only expose batch data, never real-time data
Because Salesforce cannot technically cache any ERP data locally
Because inventory and credit hold change too fast and matter too much to tolerate staleness, while catalog and price change rarely enough that a live callout would add latency for no real benefit
Because real-time callouts are always cheaper to build than batch jobs
questions.explain: The deciding factor is each field's actual volatility: fast-changing, high-stakes fields justify a live callout, while slow-changing fields are better served by a cached batch sync.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 1 case study to the integration concept it was mainly built to teach.
right: Pattern choice driven by per-field data volatility
Authentication versus authorization for an external caller
Change Data Capture versus a scheduled delta sync
questions.explain: Meridian taught matching pattern to volatility. Harborline taught idempotency under at-least-once delivery. Cascade taught why CDC closes a delta sync's blind spot. Vantage taught the authentication-versus-authorization distinction for an external, customer-scoped caller.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Harborline Capital's financial integration is designed around the standard that delivery is at-least-once, but the ________ should be exactly-once, achieved through an idempotency check on a unique transaction identifier.
questions.explain: The lesson's standard phrase is "at-least-once delivery, exactly-once effect" -- idempotency doesn't stop duplicate delivery, it makes the effect of processing a duplicate harmless.

questions.prompt: Why does a scheduled delta sync (querying by LastModifiedDate) miss a record that is created and then deleted entirely between two sync runs, while Change Data Capture does not?
options: Change Data Capture does not actually track deletions at all
A delta sync only runs once per year, so it would never catch any change
CDC and delta sync have exactly the same blind spots

A delta query only sees whatever state exists at query time, and nothing remains to match the query once the record is deleted, while CDC reacts to each individual change as it happens, including the creation before the deletion
questions.explain: A snapshot-based query run after the fact finds nothing because the record no longer exists in a changed state. CDC avoids this because it reacts to each event (including the creation) as it occurs, rather than querying a later snapshot.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Vantage Utilities external-application case study (Lesson 4).
options: Authentication verifies who is calling; authorization determines what that specific caller is allowed to do for a specific end customer
A system can be fully authenticated and still be over-permissioned if authorization isn't scoped per end user
Rate limiting exists only to defend against malicious attackers, never against a buggy retry loop in the portal's own code
API versioning lets a calling application and a Salesforce org that don't deploy on the same schedule keep working against the same integration without breaking each other
Authentication and authorization are the same question asked twice
questions.explain: Authentication and authorization are distinct questions, and a caller can pass one while failing the other. Versioning protects two independently-deployed teams from breaking each other. Rate limiting, per the lesson, most often saves an org from its own buggy client code, not only from attackers -- so that statement and the "same question" statement are both false.

questions.prompt: Which update-loop prevention technique does Bellwood Apparel's marketing-platform design (Lesson 5) use, and why?
options: Field-level change detection with a cooldown, because source-system tags are technically impossible to implement
A source-system tag marking which system originated a change, chosen because it's simpler to reason about and addresses the loop at its root cause
Disabling all synchronization permanently
Randomly delaying every sync job by several hours
questions.explain: The lesson names two valid techniques and states Bellwood's design uses the source-system tag specifically because it's simpler to reason about and catches the loop at its root cause, rather than detecting it after the fact.

questions.prompt: What does "blast radius" mean in the context of comparing integration designs?
options: How much of the system fails or degrades when one dependency fails
The physical distance between two data centers
The total number of fields included in an integration
How many developers are needed to build the integration
The dollar cost of the cloud infrastructure involved
How many test cases a QA team writes for the integration
questions.explain: Blast radius measures how much of a system is affected when one dependency fails -- it's a resilience concept, not a measure of team size, cost, distance, or field count.
questions.distractorExplain: Option C, the number of fields, describes scope or complexity, not failure impact. A design could touch very few fields and still have a huge blast radius if that handful of fields sits at the center of every critical workflow.

questions.prompt: Select every category from this course's reusable failure-mode checklist (Lesson 7).
options: Timeout
Partial failure
Duplicate delivery
Browser incompatibility
Out-of-order delivery
Silent data loss
questions.explain: The checklist's five categories are timeout, partial failure, duplicate delivery, out-of-order delivery, and silent data loss. Browser incompatibility was never part of this course's integration failure-mode checklist.

questions.prompt: Why does this course say "the integration uses OAuth" is never a complete security answer on its own?
options: Because OAuth is not a real authentication protocol
Because OAuth answers only the authentication question -- it says nothing about the separate authorization-scope question of what a caller is then permitted to do
Because using OAuth automatically grants an integration full administrative access
Because authorization is guaranteed automatically once authentication succeeds
questions.explain: OAuth proves identity (authentication). What an authenticated caller is then allowed to do is a separate authorization-scope decision the integration's own design has to make and enforce -- OAuth alone doesn't settle it.

questions.prompt: Match each security-review question from Lesson 8's checklist to what it actually asks.
left: Data in transit and at rest
right: Whether a usable trail shows what changed, when, and by which identity
How each side proves its identity and whether credentials are stored and rotated responsibly
Whether an integration's credential has exactly the access it needs, or more
Whether data is encrypted while moving and not over-retained once stored
questions.explain: Authentication asks how identity is proven. Authorization scope asks whether access is limited to exactly what's needed (least privilege). Data in transit/at rest asks about encryption and retention. Auditability asks whether a usable change trail exists.

questions.prompt: What test does Lesson 9 give for whether an ADR's "alternatives considered" section was written honestly?
options: Whether it lists at least five alternatives regardless of whether they're realistic
Whether it was written before the decision was actually made
Whether someone who disagrees with the final decision could read it and feel their position was represented fairly, even though it lost
Whether it avoids naming any specific rejected alternative
questions.explain: The honesty test is whether a disagreeing reader would feel fairly represented. A section that only lists strawmen, or exists just to make the chosen decision look obviously correct, fails this test even if it's technically present.

questions.prompt: Put these four steps of Lesson 10's self-review pass in the order this course teaches them.
items: Name at least one real alternative and run Lesson 6's comparison honestly
Walk the design through Lesson 7's five failure categories
Walk the design through Lesson 8's four security questions
Write it up as an ADR using Lesson 9's six sections
questions.explain: The self-review pass runs comparison, then failure modes, then security, and finally captures all of that reasoning in an ADR -- each step builds on tools from the lesson whose number matches its position in the sequence.

questions.prompt: In the worked Vantage Utilities self-review example (Lesson 10), what gap did walking through the failure-mode step actually surface?
options: That the portal does not require any authentication
That Vantage Utilities has no customers
That the self-review pass found no issues of any kind
That out-of-order delivery had been named but never given a concrete fix -- only acknowledged, not actually solved
questions.explain: The worked example shows that out-of-order delivery was flagged as a risk but left unresolved in the original design -- exactly the kind of gap the self-review pass exists to catch before a live reviewer finds it.

questions.prompt: Why does Lesson 11 recommend opening a review-board presentation with the decision itself, rather than the background that led to it?
options: Because background information is never relevant to a review board
Because a live, time-boxed reviewer won't wait through extended background before learning the actual decision, and every later detail then lands as support for something already understood
Because ADRs should never include a context section
Because reviewers are not allowed to ask questions once a presentation begins
questions.explain: Unlike a written document read at the reader's own pace, a live time-boxed presentation needs the conclusion up front so later details support something the reviewer already understands, rather than building toward a reveal.

questions.prompt: Select every one of Lesson 12's four recurring reviewer objection categories.
options: "Why not the simpler alternative?"
"What happens when X fails?"
"How do you know this is secure?"
"What font did you use in the diagram?"
"What if requirements change later?"
questions.explain: The four categories are the simpler-alternative objection, the failure-mode objection, the security objection, and the future-requirements objection. Diagram font choice was never one of this course's objection categories.

questions.prompt: In Lesson 12's worked Vantage Utilities objection ("couldn't the portal just call Salesforce directly with a shared token?"), what makes the modeled response strong?
options: It denies that any simpler alternative was ever considered

It honestly names the alternative's real advantage (simpler to build) and then states the specific reason it was rejected: a browser-exposed token is readable via developer tools, failing the authorization-scope question
It refuses to answer the objection at all
It claims the simpler alternative is technically impossible to build
questions.explain: A strong response to the "why not the simpler alternative" objection names the real tradeoff honestly and gives the specific, named reason it loses -- here, a security failure on authorization scope -- rather than dismissing the alternative outright.

questions.prompt: Match each Chapter 1 case study to the recurring design question Lesson 13 says it mainly turned on.
right: Bidirectional coordination between two systems that can both originate changes
Data volatility, deciding pattern per field
Consistency requirements for the actual consumer
questions.explain: Lesson 13 maps Meridian to data volatility, Harborline to delivery guarantees and idempotency, Cascade to consistency requirements, and Bellwood to bidirectional coordination -- the handful of recurring questions underneath all five case studies.

questions.prompt: In the Lesson 14 mock review board for Northgate Health Partners, why does the design choose an event-driven update for appointment status instead of a nightly batch sync?
options: Because event-driven designs have no failure modes to consider
Because the practice-management system cannot technically support a batch export
Appointment status changes a few times per appointment and staff need to see a same-day cancellation immediately, which a once-a-day batch would delay by up to 24 hours
Because a nightly batch would be cheaper but Northgate has an unlimited integration budget
questions.explain: The scoping step reasons from actual data volatility and the real use case: a same-day cancellation needs to be visible same-day, which only an event-driven design (not a once-a-day batch) can provide.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: in the Lesson 14 mock review board, when asked about a Salesforce outage during a patient text reply, the modeled answer honestly names a real ________ in the design -- the lack of a stated maximum retry window or alert after retries are exhausted -- rather than overstating the design's coverage.
questions.explain: The mock answer explicitly admits a genuine gap (no stated maximum retry window or alerting after exhausted retries) rather than claiming the design already handles the scenario -- modeling the honest-gap-admission standard taught in Lesson 12.
